title: Spatial CAPTCHA: A Geometric Reasoning Test That Stops AI
one_liner: A procedurally-generated visual puzzle system that tests spatial understanding—a skill humans have but modern AI models lack—to catch bots while keeping humans in.
lead: Online security relies on CAPTCHAs (puzzles that only humans are supposed to solve). But modern AI models got so good at reading text and understanding images that old-fashioned CAPTCHAs no longer work. This paper asks: what can AI still not do that humans find easy? The answer: spatial reasoning—imagining how shapes move in 3D space, rotating objects mentally, understanding perspective, and handling occlusions (things hidden behind other things). Spatial CAPTCHA is a procedural generation system that automatically creates unlimited spatial puzzles testing exactly these abilities. Humans pass; current AI fails.

problem.h2: Text and images are not secure anymore
paras: A CAPTCHA is a challenge given to prove you are human: read this squiggly text, or click the images with crosswalks. These worked for years because machines could not read or see. But multi-modal AI (models that read text and images at the same time, like GPT-4o) got too good. They now pass text CAPTCHAs and image CAPTCHAs as well as or better than humans do—because the AI has learned from billions of examples of text and images on the internet.

A beginner would try: make the text more squiggly, or hide more of the objects in images. But AI just gets better at parsing scrambled text and inferring hidden things. You are in an arms race you will lose, because the bottleneck has moved. Machines learned perception—reading pixels—a long time ago. The wall today is spatial understanding: how do objects move in 3D space? Can you imagine rotating a shape? Can you tell which piece is in front?

callout.html: The system generates unlimited spatial puzzles that ask: if this shape rotates 90 degrees, or if you step sideways and look, what do you see now?

steps.text: Seven task types: reference systems (which direction is up?), perspective-taking (what if you move sideways?), mental rotation (spin this shape), occlusion (what is hidden?), multi-step visualization (combine multiple rotations).
A random algorithm creates the scene: place objects, set rotation angles, define which spatial relation answers correctly. Every puzzle is different; no memorization is possible.
Adjust how many objects, how complex the layout, how many steps of rotation. Easy has 2 objects and one rotation; hard has 5 objects and three spatial transformations.
The algorithm has the true answer baked in from the scene definition. It also generates near-miss distractors (wrong rotations, wrong perspectives) and checks they fail.

steps.b: Test humans and AI side by side
steps.text: Humans see: simple puzzles, 30 seconds per puzzle. AI (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini) gets the same puzzle, measured on how often it picks correctly within 100 seconds.

paras: Instead of text recognition or 2D image tagging, the system measures spatial reasoning: the ability to mentally manipulate 3D shapes and rotations. The paper constrains and randomizes the challenge domain to spatial tasks only—asking what is invisible to pure perception.
object.object: the challenge domain: from text/2D-image-recognition to spatial-reasoning

hidden.name: spatial reasoning gap
paras: Spatial reasoning is the mental skill to rotate objects, understand perspective, handle occlusion, and work with reference frames. It is hidden because AI does not report it; you have to measure it by asking questions. For each puzzle, the system has the ground-truth answer (encoded in the scene definition). It compares human and AI responses against that truth.

The paper estimates this gap by running the same spatial puzzles on humans and 10 leading models (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, and others). Humans averaged 97% pass rate on the easy subset; the best model reached only 31%. The gap—66 percentage points—is the reason Spatial CAPTCHA works as security. Spatial reasoning is what has not yet saturated.

heat.caption: Darker means humans excel; pale means AI lags. The gap (right side) is the target.

reads.html: Spatial reasoning is how well you can picture shapes moving in 3D: imagine this cube rotating, now which face is on top? Humans do this intuitively. AI models guess.

The paper measures Pass@1 accuracy across four spatial-ability categories and three difficulty levels. Human-Simple at easy difficulty and sample size 60 achieves 97% correct. The best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieves 29% correct on the same subset.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the three-stage pipeline
paras: Spatial CAPTCHA works because it extracts the exact gap. The system has three hardened components: (1) procedural generation ensures infinite puzzle diversity, killing memorization; (2) constraint-based difficulty control targets the gap precisely—easy puzzles have just enough spatial load to be solvable, hard puzzles pile on occlusions and multi-step rotations; (3) ground-truth certification ensures the answer is mathematically verified, not a guess. Each puzzle's correctness is computed from the scene definition itself (object positions and rotations), so distractors are provably wrong.

Here is why AI fails while humans pass: humans have intuitive spatial understanding from living in a 3D world. When they see a rotated cube, they immediately picture where each face moved. AI models were trained on the internet—lots of text and 2D images, but relatively few 3D-reasoning scenarios and hardly any procedurally-generated spatial puzzles. So when asked to rotate a shape or account for an occlusion, the AI model is guessing a pattern from its training, not actually reasoning spatially.

stages.s: Task type: rotate a cube 90 degrees. Difficulty level: hard (5 objects, 2 rotations).
Procedural generator: randomize object positions, rotation angles, and visual style.
Constraint enforcement: ensure objects do not overlap, maintain legibility, make answer unique.
Distractor generation: create near-miss answers (wrong rotation, wrong perspective).
Ground-truth certification: compute the correct answer from object positions and rotations, verify distractors fail.
A puzzle: image plus four multiple-choice answers. Humans answer intuitively; AI guess-patterns fail.

symbols: difficulty score for the scene parameters
the input knobs: object count, rotation steps, occlusion fraction, layout complexity
features extracted from those knobs, e.g. (count, max_rotations, occlusion_depth)
learned weights: importance of each feature, fitted to human response times

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scene A: 2 objects, 1 rotation, no occlusion -> ϕ(A) = (2, 1, 0) -> d(A) = 0.3*2 + 0.5*1 + 0.2*0 = 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1 (easy)
The weights are fitted so that d=1.1 correlates with ~90% human pass rate and d=3.5 with ~60%. Difficulty controls the spatial load, not the visual noise.

math.note: Difficulty is a linear combination of scene features, tuned so that easy puzzles have one transformation and hard puzzles layer spatial operations.

charts.note: AI rivals humans on image tagging. Weakening rapidly.

charts.title: Spatial CAPTCHA (this paper)
charts.note: Spatial reasoning is where AI lags. The gap persists across all 10 tested models.

items.html: If the random placement algorithm leaves obvious visual patterns (all objects in a line, or all at the same depth), an AI could learn those shortcuts instead of doing spatial reasoning. The paper prevents this with constraint-based generation: objects must be spread, occlusions must vary, rendering must avoid consistent bias.

items.b: Distractors are too easy to rule out.
items.html: If the wrong answers are obviously wrong (a cube clearly in the wrong orientation), the AI does not have to reason spatially; it just eliminates noise. The paper controls this by generating near-miss distractors: the wrong perspective is plausible, the mismatched rotation is subtle, the hidden piece count is off by one.

items.b: AI trains on spatial reasoning data.
items.html: If a new model is trained on millions of 3D scenes, procedurally-generated spatial puzzles, and multi-step rotations, the gap will shrink. The paper is a benchmark today; it will be a regression test tomorrow. The system must evolve.

items.b: Done right: humans validate ground truth.
items.html: The paper includes human-in-the-loop validation: 60 human raters review puzzles to ensure the ground truth is actually correct and the distractors are plausible. This guards against bugs in the procedural generator.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a procedural generator that creates three spatial task types (mental rotation, perspective-taking, occlusion). For each task, generate 20 random scenes at three difficulty levels. Render each as an image plus four multiple-choice answers. Then: ask 10 humans (or yourself) to solve them, recording pass rate and response time. Next, submit the same image and options to an AI model (like Claude or GPT-4o) and log its answers. Compare side by side.
demo.closing: If the metric is +60 percentage points or higher, the spatial reasoning gap is real and measured, not theoretical.
